To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the familial risk for cancer is higher than the risk in the general population and that the risk increases with the number of affected first-degree relatives and with the age of the affected relative.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the familial risks for cancer, and their implications for the clinical practice and counseling of patients.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that control the development of the nervous system.
the development of evidence-based clinical referral guidelines, based on familial risks for cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence does not support the use of vitamin E supplements in the general population to reduce cancer risk.
the risk of cancer in a first-degree relative (parent, sibling or child) with breast cancer is approximately twice that of the general population.
there is no evidence for the existence of a gene for familial breast cancer, and the evidence for a gene for familial ovarian cancer is not convincing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the family history of cancer is a powerful tool for cancer prevention, and the most important risk factors for the most prevalent cancers are now known.
familial cancer is an important public health concern.
the family cancer history is a powerful tool to identify high-risk individuals for cancer screening, surveillance, and genetic counseling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of cancer is not just a function of your age and sex, but also your family history.
we have developed a new method of detecting the presence of the cancer-associated gene, BRCA1, in the blood of women at high risk of breast cancer.
there are familial risks for many cancers.
